peatanddeadwood-handbook-peat-text: Peat burns cool. Dried peat tops out at 145°C and fresh peat at 95°C - both are far below what meat, fish, poultry or bread need to cook, and fresh peat cannot even bring a pot to a boil. This is not a bug: the same number that sets how hot a fire burns also stands in for how clean it burns, and peat is a smoky, sooty fuel that never gets hot enough to cook flesh at any tech level. Vegetable and grain dishes still cook in a pot, just slower than on wood. A clay oven is unaffected by fuel temperature, so peat bakes bread there exactly as well as anything else. What peat is good for: heating a room, and doing it for a very long time from cheap, dug-up bulk fuel. Season a summer's digging in a shed and you will never run short of warmth - just don't expect dinner from it.
peatanddeadwood-handbook-preheat-title: Preheating: Banking Heat Before You Switch Fuels
peatanddeadwood-handbook-preheat-text: A firepit's temperature carries over when you change fuel - it does not reset. That means burning a hot softwood split first, then switching to charcoal, gives the charcoal a head start: it does not have to climb from cold, and the climb is not linear, so heat already banked is heat charcoal never has to pay for again. One split of a hot, fast softwood before charcoal saves roughly half a charcoal's worth of burn time - worth doing on every cold start. Insert the item you're actually smelting or smithing *before* you swap in the charcoal, not after. The firepit gives idle fuel a 4x burn-time bonus whenever there's nothing in the input slot and the fire is near its target temperature - exactly the state right after a hot preheat split. Swap fuel first with an empty input and that bonus can stall your charcoal swap for up to four times as long as the split should have taken. Load the crucible or ore first, then swap the fuel, and the bonus never triggers.
peatanddeadwood-handbook-pitkiln-title: Pit Kiln: The Top Layer Sets the Clock
peatanddeadwood-handbook-pitkiln-text: A pit kiln takes four fuel layers, but only one of them controls how long the firing takes: whichever fuel you place *last* sets the burn time for the whole kiln, overwriting whatever the layers below it would have used. The other three layers can be built from anything - cheap wet wood, deadwood, whatever's on hand - and only the final layer's fuel matters for timing. If you want dried peat's shorter firing, dried peat needs to be the last thing you place, not just present somewhere in the stack.
